title: "Chapter 3: Digital Watermarking"

## Overview

Digital watermarking consists of embedding invisible information — a message or signature — directly into multimedia content (image, video, audio) so that it persists despite modifications. Applications range from copyright protection to broadcast monitoring, steganography, and tamper detection. The fundamental pipeline relies on a trio: an **embedder**, a potentially hostile channel, and a **decoder** that recovers the message or verifies the presence of the watermark using the secret key.

## Chapter Synthesis {#synthesis}

::: {.callout-note title="Fundamental Trade-offs"}
Every digital watermarking system must balance four antagonistic properties:

- **Robustness**: the watermark survives compression, cropping, geometric attacks.
- **Imperceptibility**: the visual quality of the watermarked image remains high (PSNR $> 40$ dB).
- **Capacity**: number of bits $L$ that can be embedded.
- **Security**: resistance to an adversary who knows the algorithm but not the key.

**Additive embedding model (zero-bit):**
$$\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \varepsilon\mathbf{w}, \quad \mathbf{w} = \text{Gen}(k), \quad \|\mathbf{w}\| = 1$$

**Detection score:**
$$S(\mathbf{v}) = \frac{1}{M}\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}$$

**Hypothesis test:**

- $H_0$: $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}$ (no watermark) → $\mathbb{E}[S] = 0$
- $H_1$: $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x} + \varepsilon\mathbf{w}$ (watermark present) → $\mathbb{E}[S] = \varepsilon$

**L-bit watermark:** $\hat{m} = g(\mathbf{v}, k)$, $m \in \{0,1\}^L$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Main Applications"}
| Application | Type | Principle |
|:-----------|:-----|:---------|
| Copyright protection | Zero-bit / L-bit | Identify the work or its owner |
| Broadcast monitoring | L-bit | Track content distribution |
| Steganography | L-bit | Secret communication channel in image |
| Tamper detection | Fragile | Fragile watermark localized by region |
| Fingerprinting | L-bit | Identify the acquirer (traceability) |
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Embedding Domains"}
| Domain | Transform | Robustness | Notes |
|:-------|:---------|:---------|:------|
| Pixel | None | Low | Simple, sensitive to geometric attacks |
| DCT | Discrete cosine | Good | JPEG-compatible, mid-frequency coefficients |
| DWT | Discrete wavelets | Very good | Multi-resolution, perceptual masking |
| Deep features | CNN/ViT | Excellent | End-to-end optimization, very robust |
:::

## Introduction to Digital Watermarking

Digital watermarking aims to make content **self-authenticating** by concealing information that will accompany the work throughout its digital life. Unlike electronic signatures, the watermark is tied to the signal itself rather than its metadata.

General pipeline:
$$\mathbf{y} = \omega(\mathbf{x}, k, m), \qquad \hat{m} = g(\mathbf{v}, k)$$

where $\mathbf{v} = \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y})$ denotes the received image after channel / attacks $\mathcal{A}$.

The embedding strength $\varepsilon$ directly controls the robustness–imperceptibility trade-off:

$$D_{xy} = \frac{1}{M}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^2 = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{M}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = \varepsilon^2 \quad (\text{if } \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = M)$$

$$\text{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{255^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right) \text{ [dB]}$$
